title: The desert houses
hook: Carmelites keep times of deep silence and solitude

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's counsels: short sayings for daily life, like in the evening you will be examined on love. Your line was counsels. Which saying did you carry? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

Mark's Gospel describes a long day in Capernaum. Jesus heals a fever, and by sunset the whole town seems to be crowded at the door with its sick. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." His friends come hunting for him, and when they find him, they say it plainly: "All seek for thee." Before the next town, before the next crowd, he goes to a quiet place first. Carmelites took that pattern and gave it buildings. Today is those buildings.
screen: `A CROWDED DAY IN CAPERNAUM.` → `VERY EARLY, A DESERT PLACE.` → `ALL SEEK FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: A desert, in Carmelite language, doesn't need sand. It's a place set apart for silence and solitude. In the reformed branch of the order, friars founded houses they called deserts, set apart from busy places, where a friar could withdraw for a season and live closer to the hermits of the first Carmel: a cell, long hours of prayer, very little talk. The idea comes straight out of the Rule from a few days ago. The Rule asks for silence, and it quotes the prophet Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "in silence and in hope shall your strength be." Silence there isn't emptiness. It's where strength is gathered. The prophet Hosea gives the desert a tenderness, too. God says of his people: "I will allure her, and will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart." The wilderness is where the speaking happens, because nothing else is talking. Some Carmelite communities still keep desert days and times of deeper retreat, and lay people who follow Carmel sometimes make their own. Notice the rhythm, though. Jesus goes to the desert place, and then he goes back out, to the next towns. The desert isn't an escape from people. It's a return to the source so you have something to give them. A desert house may be far away. But an hour without noise, a walk without headphones, a room with the door shut, can do a small version of the same work.
screen: `A DESERT DOESN'T NEED SAND.` · `HOUSES SET APART FOR SILENCE.` · `I WILL SPEAK TO HER HEART.` · `INTO THE DESERT, THEN BACK OUT.` · then, large: `IN SILENCE AND IN HOPE SHALL YOUR STRENGTH BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small desert now, and a bigger one later. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, let everything go quiet: no music, no screen, no plans. If you pray, you can rest in Isaiah's words, in silence and in hope, and let God speak first. If you don't, just listen to how loud the quiet is. Then, before the bell, choose one hour later today or this week to keep in silence, and decide where it will be. The bell holds the time.
The desert houses. Carmelite places set apart for deep silence and solitude, the hermit life of the first Carmel, kept alive. Today's word.
Your line: the desert. Today, keep the hour you chose. If an hour isn't possible, keep twenty minutes, phone in another room. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Carmelite communities keep regular times of deeper silence and solitude, sometimes called desert days, and some Carmelite friars have houses set apart for longer periods of retreat.

what a scholar hears: the reform's friars founded 'deserts' to recover the hermit life of the Rule, which itself quotes Isaiah on silence and hope.

notes: The Discalced friars' 'deserts' (houses of solitude) are described generally, with no names, dates or counts; confirm the description ('usually far from towns', 'withdraw for a season').
Carmelite communities keeping desert days, and lay Carmelites making their own: confirm.
The Rule's silence chapter quoting Isaiah 30:15 to confirm.
Hosea 2:14 numbering: in the Douay-Rheims this may be Osee 2:14; confirm verse and wording. Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 1:35, 1:37 and Isaiah 30:15 to confirm.
'By sunset the whole town seems to be crowded at the door' paraphrases Mark 1:32–33.

Editor: 'usually far from towns' softened to 'set apart from busy places'; 'Carmelite communities still keep' narrowed to 'some'; stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' cut; the fork no longer asks the listener to play Jesus and instead puts them among the friends who go looking for him (Mark 1:36–37).
Original: Latin Vulgate Isaiah 30:15 'in silentio et in spe erit fortitudo vestra'; confirm wording and that the Rule quotes it.
